claim: Using computer simulations, the authors generate cell-specific 3D chromosomal structures and compare them to recently published chromatin structures obtained through microscopy.
source: Using computer simulations, we generate cell-specific 3D chromosomal structures and compare them to recently published chromatin structures obtained through microscopy.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a description of the study's methodology.

claim: Epigenetic information can be used to predict the structural ensembles of multiple human cell lines using machine learning and polymer physics simulations.
source: We demonstrate using machine learning and polymer physics simulations that epigenetic information can be used to predict the structural ensembles of multiple human cell lines.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated throughout the manuscript with simulations.

claim: Theory predicts that chromosome structures are fluid and can only be described by an ensemble.
source: Theory predicts that chromosome structures are fluid and can only be described by an ensemble, which is consistent with the observation that chromosomes exhibit no unique fold.
evidence: This theoretical prediction is stated in the abstract and supported by the energy landscape model.

claim: Chromosomes exhibit no unique fold.
source: Theory predicts that chromosome structures are fluid and can only be described by an ensemble, which is consistent with the observation that chromosomes exhibit no unique fold.
evidence: This is stated as an observation consistent with theoretical predictions.

claim: Short segments of chromatin make two-state transitions between closed conformations and open dumbbell conformations.
source: Nevertheless, our analysis of both structures from simulation and microscopy reveals that short segments of chromatin make two-state transitions between closed conformations and open dumbbell conformations.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through clustering analysis in the results.

claim: The formation of genomic compartments resembles hydrophobic collapse in protein folding.
source: The formation of genomic compartments resembles hydrophobic collapse in protein folding, with the aggregation of denser and predominantly inactive chromatin driving the positioning of active chromatin toward the surface of individual chromosomal territories.
evidence: This analogy is explicitly stated in the abstract and discussed in the results section.

claim: The aggregation of denser and predominantly inactive chromatin drives the positioning of active chromatin toward the surface of individual chromosomal territories.
source: The formation of genomic compartments resembles hydrophobic collapse in protein folding, with the aggregation of denser and predominantly inactive chromatin driving the positioning of active chromatin toward the surface of individual chromosomal territories.
evidence: This mechanism is stated in the abstract and demonstrated through radial density analysis.

claim: The 3D spatial organization of chromosomes in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells appears to be cell-type-specific.
source: The 3D spatial organization of the chromosomes in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells appears to be cell-type-specific (Rao et al., 2014; Dixon et al., 2012; Dixon et al., 2015; Rowley et al., 2017; Dekker and Heard, 2015; Yu and Ren, 2017; Tang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: DNA–DNA ligation experiments have revealed spatial compartmentalization, generally termed A/B compartmentalization.
source: DNA–DNA ligation experiments have revealed spatial compartmentalization, generally termed A/B compartmentalization (Lieberman-Aiden et al., 2009), and CTCF-mediated loop domains.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to the original work describing A/B compartmentalization.

claim: The A compartment chromatin contains a larger amount of the expressed genes while the B compartment chromatin is less transcriptionally active.
source: It was observed that the A compartment chromatin contains a larger amount of the expressed genes while the B compartment chromatin is less transcriptionally active.
evidence: This is stated as an established observation in the introduction.

claim: Similar A/B compartmentalization has been observed across human cell lines as well as in other species, suggesting that compartmentalization is a conserved feature of genome organization across evolution.
source: Similar A/B compartmentalization has been observed across human cell lines (Rao et al., 2014; Dixon et al., 2012; Dixon et al., 2015) as well as in other species (Dixon et al., 2012; Rowley et al., 2017; Dudchenko and Shamim, 2018; Sexton et al., 2012; Eagen et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2012), suggesting that compartmentalization is a conserved feature of genome organization across evolution.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations across different species.

claim: Recent microscopy approaches have begun to reveal the 3D structures of segments of chromatin longer than a megabase at a spatial resolution on the nanometer scale.
source: Recent microscopy approaches have begun to reveal the 3D structures of segments of chromatin longer than a megabase at a spatial resolution on the nanometer scale (Bintu et al., 2018; Boettiger et al., 2016; Nir et al., 2018; Beliveau et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to recent microscopy studies.

claim: One consistent observation from imaging approaches and single-cell DNA–DNA ligation experiments has been the high degree of structural variability seen within an apparently homogeneous population of synchronized cells of a single-cell type.
source: One consistent observation from the imaging approaches, as well as from single-cell DNA–DNA ligation experiments (Nagano et al., 2013; Stevens et al., 2017; Tan et al., 2018; Finn et al., 2019), has been the high degree of structural variability seen within an apparently homogeneous population of synchronized cells of a single-cell type.
evidence: This observation is stated with multiple citations supporting it.

claim: Well-defined cell-type-specific DNA–DNA ligation maps for the ensemble emerge after population averaging the single-cell results.
source: Despite this variability, well-defined cell-type-specific DNA–DNA ligation maps for the ensemble emerge after population averaging the single-cell results.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about population-averaged data.

claim: The Minimal Chromatin Model (MiChroM) has been shown to accurately predict the population-averaged DNA–DNA ligation maps.
source: In particular, the Minimal Chromatin Model (MiChroM) has been shown to accurately predict the population-averaged DNA–DNA ligation maps (Di Pierro et al., 2016; Di Pierro et al., 2017; Di Pierro et al., 2018; Contessoto et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous work validating the model.

claim: The propensity toward phase separation for chromosomes of human lymphoblastoid cells can be reliably predicted using epigenetic marking data.
source: The propensity toward phase separation for chromosomes of human lymphoblastoid cells can be reliably predicted using epigenetic marking data (Di Pierro et al., 2017), suggesting that the information contained within the 1D epigenetic marking patterns decorating the chromatin polymer is sufficient to predict the ensemble of 3D chromosome structures.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work.

claim: The information contained within the 1D epigenetic marking patterns decorating the chromatin polymer is sufficient to predict the ensemble of 3D chromosome structures.
source: The propensity toward phase separation for chromosomes of human lymphoblastoid cells can be reliably predicted using epigenetic marking data (Di Pierro et al., 2017), suggesting that the information contained within the 1D epigenetic marking patterns decorating the chromatin polymer is sufficient to predict the ensemble of 3D chromosome structures.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion based on previous findings.

claim: MEGABASE was trained to quantify the statistical relationship between the experimental sub-compartment annotations and the histone methylation and acetylation markings tracks.
source: A neural network called MEGABASE (Di Pierro et al., 2017) was trained to quantify the statistical relationship between the experimental sub-compartment annotations and the histone methylation and acetylation markings tracks, as assayed using chromatin immunoprecipitation data.
evidence: This describes the training of the MEGABASE neural network.

claim: MEGABASE can be used to predict the compartmentalization patterns of a chromosome using a set of epigenetic ChIP-Seq tracks as the sole input.
source: Once trained, MEGABASE can be used to predict the compartmentalization patterns of a chromosome using a set of epigenetic ChIP-Seq tracks as the sole input.
evidence: This describes the capability of the trained MEGABASE model.

claim: The authors generated predictions for cell lines HMEC, HUVEC, IMR90, K562, HeLa-S3, and H1-hESC using the MEGABASE+MiChroM computational pipeline.
source: Using the MEGABASE neural network, which was previously trained using data from GM12878, and sourcing from the Encyclopedia of DNA Elements (ENCODE) database the ChIP-Seq tracks for the same 11 histone modifications previously used, sub-compartment annotations for all the autosomes of cell lines were generated that had never been used in the training phase of the neural network. These sequences of sub-compartment annotations, or chromatin types, then serve as input for molecular dynamics simulations using the Minimal Chromatin Model (MiChroM) (Di Pierro et al., 2016). Using this combined approach, the chromosomal structural ensembles for six additional cell lines were generated: human fetal lung cells (IMR-90), human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVEC), immortalized myelogenous leukemia cells (K562), human mammary epithelial cells (HMEC), human embryonic stem cells (H1-hESC), and HeLa-S3 cells.
evidence: This describes the application of the computational pipeline to multiple cell lines.

claim: For each cell type, averaging the simulated ensemble generates in silico DNA–DNA ligation maps, which are consistent with those determined experimentally.
source: For each cell type, averaging the simulated ensemble generates in silico DNA–DNA ligation maps, which are consistent with those determined experimentally.
evidence: This is stated as a result and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The Pearson's R between the simulated and experimental maps of matching cell type shows that the long-range patterns of compartmentalization are captured over tens of mega-bases.
source: In particular, the Pearson's R between the simulated and experimental maps of matching cell type as a function of genomic distance shows that the long-range patterns of compartmentalization are captured over tens of mega-bases.
evidence: This is stated as a result of the comparison analysis.

claim: Computational modeling delineates the difference between cell type and appears to best match the experimental map when the cell types of simulation and experiment are matched up.
source: While the experimental observations on different cell lines do correlate with each other, computational modeling delineates the difference between cell type and appears to best match the experimental map when the cell types of simulation and experiment are matched up.
evidence: This is stated as a result of comparing matching and mismatching cell types.

claim: The theoretical model discriminates well between different cell lines.
source: This last result demonstrates that the present theoretical model discriminates well between different cell lines.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the comparison analysis.

claim: The inclusion of CTCF-loops improves the quality of the results for the short range features of chromosome organization within 10 Mb in genomic distance.
source: Figure 1D shows that the inclusion of CTCF-loops, which are easily be incorporated into the model, improves the quality of the results for the short range features of chromosome organization within 10 Mb in genomic distance; at larger length scales the model appears to be completely insensitive of CTCF-mediated loops.
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 1D.

claim: At larger length scales (>10 Mb), the model appears to be completely insensitive of CTCF-mediated loops.
source: Figure 1D shows that the inclusion of CTCF-loops, which are easily be incorporated into the model, improves the quality of the results for the short range features of chromosome organization within 10 Mb in genomic distance; at larger length scales the model appears to be completely insensitive of CTCF-mediated loops.
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 1D.

claim: Long-range compartmentalization observed in the DNA–DNA ligation maps is well captured by the simulated structural ensembles for these well-studied cell lines using only information about the epigenetic marking patterns as input.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that long-range compartmentalization observed in the DNA–DNA ligation maps is well captured by the simulated structural ensembles for these well-studied cell lines using only information about the epigenetic marking patterns as input.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the results.

claim: Unlike the situation for folded globular proteins, chromatin appears to be highly dynamical and cannot be characterized by any single conformation.
source: It has become increasingly clear that unlike the situation for folded globular proteins, which typically can be reasonably well approximated for many purposes by a single native structure corresponding to the average conformation, chromatin appears to be highly dynamical and cannot be characterized by any single conformation.
evidence: This is stated as an established understanding in the field.

claim: The heterogeneity of the chromosomal structural ensembles was first suggested by the analysis of the free energy landscape of chromosomes.
source: The heterogeneity of the chromosomal structural ensembles was first suggested by the analysis of the free energy landscape of chromosomes (Zhang and Wolynes, 2015; Di Pierro et al., 2016) and has been indirectly observed through single-cell DNA–DNA ligation experiments (Nagano et al., 2013; Stevens et al., 2017; Tan et al., 2018; Finn et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with citations to the relevant work.

claim: The heterogeneity of chromosomal structural ensembles has been confirmed by direct imaging of individual chromosomal structures.
source: The heterogeneity has now been confirmed by direct imaging of individual chromosomal structures (Bintu et al., 2018; Boettiger et al., 2016; Nir et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations to imaging studies.

claim: Statistical ensembles must be used in order to describe chromosomal structures in vivo due to conformational plasticity.
source: As a consequence of this conformational plasticity, statistical ensembles (Zhang and Wolynes, 2015; Di Pierro et al., 2016; Di Pierro et al., 2017; Di Pierro et al., 2018; Zhang and Wolynes, 2016; Di Pierro, 2019; Goundaroulis et al., 2020; Bascom et al., 2019; Dekker et al., 2013; Kalhor et al., 2012) must be used in order to describe chromosomal structures in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of conformational plasticity with supporting citations.

claim: The traced structures can be used to generate a population-averaged contact maps, which turn out to be consistent with DNA–DNA ligation maps.
source: As previously reported (Bintu et al., 2018; Boettiger et al., 2016; Nir et al., 2018), the traced structures can be used to generate a population-averaged contact maps, which turn out to be consistent with DNA–DNA ligation maps.
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous reports.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of the traced structures for Segment 1 yields three distinct clusters: a closed dumbbell, an open dumbbell, and a highly dense chromatin state.
source: When applied to the 936 combined experimental structures for Segment 1, the clustering algorithm yields three distinct clusters. These correspond to a closed dumbbell (Cluster 1), an open dumbbell (Cluster 2), and a highly dense chromatin state (Cluster 3) shown in Figure 2.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Seven dense, highly compact structures were identified from clustering.
source: Additionally, seven dense, highly compact structures were identified from clustering.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the clustering analysis.

claim: The relative number of open and closed structures found in the simulations is in remarkable agreement with the experimental finding.
source: Interestingly, the relative number of open and closed structures found in the simulations (discussed in the next section) is in remarkable agreement with this experimental finding.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between simulation and experiment.

claim: The vast majority of genes appear to be positioned along the linker region connecting the two globular domains of Segment 1.
source: Interestingly, the vast majority of genes appear to be positioned along the linker region connecting the two globular domains (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Segment 2 of IMR90 completely lacks loop domains.
source: Unlike Segment 1, Segment 2 of IMR90 completely lacks loop domains and, consequently, the averaged contact maps for Segment 2 exhibit no additional features beyond the decay in contact probability as a function of genomic distance (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Without the presence of loop domains, Segment 2 is highly disordered.
source: Structural analysis reveals that, without the presence of loop domains, Segment 2 is highly disordered; while clustering reveals open and closed structures, the lack of loop domains and domain boundaries results in the loss of dumbbell-like structures (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Unlike Segment 1, Segment 2 has an absence of genes.
source: It should be noted that unlike Segment 1, Segment 2 has an absence of genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The conformational states observed using microscopy are also found in the simulated structural ensemble without any calibration or fine tuning of parameters.
source: We compare the chromosome structures sampled in the simulations to the diffraction-limited microscopy structures of Bintu et al., 2018, finding that the conformational states observed using microscopy are also found in the simulated structural ensemble without any calibration or fine tuning of parameters.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding comparing simulation to experiment.

claim: The simulated model and the structural variability that it captures was derived from the energy landscape learned from population-averaged DNA–DNA ligation data using the principle of maximum entropy.
source: It is important to note that the simulated model, and the structural variability that it captures, was derived from the energy landscape learned from population-averaged DNA–DNA ligation data using the principle of maximum entropy (Di Pierro et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the methodology used to derive the model.

claim: The closed and open structures from simulation are consistent with those observed in the Bintu et al., 2018 datasets.
source: The closed and open structures are consistent with those observed in the Bintu et al., 2018 datasets.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between simulation and experiment.

claim: No highly dense structures exist in the simulations.
source: No highly dense structures exist in the simulations. Such structures would collapse the entire chromatin segment to the volume of a single monomer, an occurrence that is prohibited by the energy function used to model the system.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the simulation model.

claim: The view that Cluster 3 seen in the experiments are artifacts is in harmony with the absence of highly dense structures in simulations.
source: This is in harmony with our view that Cluster 3 seen in the experiments are artifacts of some sort.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation consistent with the simulation results.

claim: The free energy difference between open and closed states in simulation is remarkably consistent with the value estimated using only the experimentally traced structures.
source: This free energy difference is remarkably consistent with the value estimated using only the experimentally traced structures in the preceding section.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between simulation and experiment.

claim: Any discrepancies between the experimental and simulated datasets can be captured within 5% error of the original length estimate.
source: It is particularly remarkable that any discrepancies between the experimental and simulated datasets can in fact be captured within 5% error of our original length estimate (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Certain loci have similar epigenetic markings patterns in all the cell types examined, either by being generally transcriptionally active loci or by being transcriptionally inactive B compartment loci.
source: It is evident that certain loci have similar epigenetic markings patterns in all the cell types that we examined, either by being generally transcriptionally active loci, thus likely belonging to the A compartment, or by being transcriptionally inactive B compartment loci.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Several segments of chromatin switch compartments between different cell types.
source: On the other hand, several segments of chromatin switch compartments between different cell types.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the analysis.

claim: A compartment loci tend to localize toward the surface of the chromosome.
source: Taking a look at the radial distance of the center of mass of the segment of chromatin in each of the cell types, one finds that the A compartment loci tend to localize toward the surface of the chromosome, while the B compartment loci of the HUVEC cell type tend to localize in the interior (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: B compartment loci tend to localize in the interior of the chromosome.
source: Taking a look at the radial distance of the center of mass of the segment of chromatin in each of the cell types, one finds that the A compartment loci tend to localize toward the surface of the chromosome, while the B compartment loci of the HUVEC cell type tend to localize in the interior (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: A similar positioning of transcriptionally active chromatin toward the periphery of chromosomal territories was observed by Nagano et al., 2013 in mouse cells using Hi-C experiments.
source: A similar positioning of transcriptionally active chromatin toward the periphery of chromosomal territories was also observed by Nagano et al., 2013 in mouse cells using Hi-C experiments.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the observation.

claim: According to the MiChroM potential, contact interactions between B loci exhibit the most favorable energetic stabilization of all chromatin interactions.
source: The finding that there exists a radial ordering associated with the spatial compartmentalization is consistent with the fact that according to the MiChroM potential (Di Pierro et al., 2016), contact interactions between B loci exhibit the most favorable energetic stabilization of all chromatin interactions.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the MiChroM model.

claim: A to B or A to A-type interactions are comparably strong to each other, but are significantly weaker than the B to B interaction.
source: On the other hand, A to B or A to A-type interactions are comparably strong to each other, but are significantly weaker than the B to B interaction (See Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the MiChroM model parameters.

claim: According to the MiChroM energetic parameters, B loci drive the phase separation of the chromosomes.
source: In other words, according to the MiChroM energetic parameters (which were originally learned from Hi-C maps), B loci drive the phase separation of the chromosomes.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the model parameters.

claim: The B compartmentalization forms the stable core of the simulated chromosome.
source: Much like a hydrophobic-polar model from protein folding, the B compartmentalization forms the stable core of the simulated chromosome and the weaker interactions between A compartment loci with A or B loci tends toward the surface, to minimize the free energy of the molecular assembly.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the simulation results.

claim: The weaker interactions between A compartment loci with A or B loci tend toward the surface, to minimize the free energy of the molecular assembly.
source: Much like a hydrophobic-polar model from protein folding, the B compartmentalization forms the stable core of the simulated chromosome and the weaker interactions between A compartment loci with A or B loci tends toward the surface, to minimize the free energy of the molecular assembly.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the simulation results.

claim: The theoretical model corroborates recent experiments that suggest heterochromatin phase separation is a major driving force behind genome organization.
source: Our theoretical model thus corroborates recent experiments (Falk et al., 2019; Strom et al., 2017) that suggests heterochromatin phase separation is a major driving force behind genome organization, further highlighting the important role of phase separation in biological organization (Di Pierro et al., 2016; Hnisz et al., 2017; Brangwynne et al., 2015; Banani et al., 2016; Shin and Brangwynne, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion with supporting citations.

claim: DNA-tracing combined with diffraction-limited or super-resolution microscopy is beginning to shed light on the high degree of variability that is characteristic of chromosomal structures in the interphase.
source: DNA-tracing combined with diffraction-limited or super-resolution microscopy is beginning to shed light on the high degree of variability that is characteristic of chromosomal structures in the interphase (Bintu et al., 2018; Boettiger et al., 2016; Nir et al., 2018; Beliveau et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to recent microscopy studies.

claim: A unique chromosomal fold simply does not exist in the interphase.
source: These studies add to the growing body of evidence that a unique chromosomal fold simply does not exist in the interphase.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the growing body of evidence.

claim: Chromosome structures in the nucleus appear to be highly dynamical, owing to the many non-equilibrium processes in the cell, such as the activity of motor proteins.
source: Chromosome structures in the nucleus appear to be highly dynamical, owing to the many non-equilibrium processes in the cell, such as the activity of motor proteins.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the dynamical nature of chromosome structures.

claim: The collective variable Q, commonly used in protein folding studies and structural biophysics, is suitable for characterizing the structural ensemble of a segment of chromatin.
source: Our results demonstrate that the collective variable Q, commonly used in protein folding studies and structural biophysics, is suitable for characterizing the structural ensemble of a segment of chromatin.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: For segments of chromatin as short as ~2 Mb in length, there do exist distinct clusters of chromatin structures that can be distinguished using Q.
source: Despite the high degree of conformational plasticity, it appears that for segments of chromatin as short as the ones imaged by Bintu et al., 2018 (~2 Mb in length), there do exist distinct clusters of chromatin structures that can be distinguished using Q.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the clustering analysis.

claim: The dominant structures found for chromatin Segment 1 can be described as being a closed dumbbell and an open dumbbell, where the ends of the dumbbell are the globular domains at the head and tail of the chromatin segment.
source: The dominant structures found for chromatin Segment 1 (chr21 29.37–31.32 Mb) examined using data from microscopy as well as from simulation can be described as being a closed dumbbell and an open dumbbell, where the ends of the dumbbell are the globular domains at the head and tail of the chromatin segment.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the dominant structures.

claim: CTCF proteins bound along the genome act as gene insulators, probably through their suppressing activity toward loop extrusion.
source: It is known that CTCF proteins bound along the genome act as gene insulators, probably through their suppressing activity toward loop extrusion (Sanborn et al., 2015; Fudenberg et al., 2016; Vian et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as known information with supporting citations.

claim: Classification of the experimentally imaged structures of Segment 2 lack the domain boundaries that segregate the head and the tail of the chromatin segment into globular domains, although still exhibiting open and closed conformations.
source: Classification of the experimentally imaged structures of Segment 2 lack the domain boundaries that segregate the head and the tail of the chromatin segment into globular domains, although still exhibiting open and closed conformations.
evidence: This is stated as a result of the structural analysis.

claim: These findings suggest a possible role in transcriptional regulation for the opening and closing of organized dumbbell structures.
source: These findings suggest a possible role in transcriptional regulation for the opening and closing of organized dumbbell structures.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the findings.

claim: Understanding the structure-function relationship in the genome is a crucial question that can only be answered using an accurate statistical characterization of the conformational ensembles.
source: It is however clear that understanding the structure-function relationship in the genome is a crucial question that can only be answered using an accurate statistical characterization of the conformational ensembles.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the importance of ensemble characterization.

claim: The theoretical model MiChroM predicts that transcriptionally active loci, typically belonging to the A compartment, move toward the surface of the chromosomal territory.
source: Finally, our work refines the classical view of the spatial compartmentalization of chromatin. We find a striking dependence between radial positioning of chromatin and epigenetic marking patterns. Our theoretical model, MiChroM, predicts that transcriptionally active loci, typically belonging to the A compartment, move toward the surface of the chromosomal territory, while B compartment loci, typically inactive, move to the interior (Di Pierro et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the theoretical model.

claim: B compartment loci, typically inactive, move to the interior of the chromosomal territory.
source: Finally, our work refines the classical view of the spatial compartmentalization of chromatin. We find a striking dependence between radial positioning of chromatin and epigenetic marking patterns. Our theoretical model, MiChroM, predicts that transcriptionally active loci, typically belonging to the A compartment, move toward the surface of the chromosomal territory, while B compartment loci, typically inactive, move to the interior (Di Pierro et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the theoretical model.

claim: Aggregation of B loci seems to be the driving force behind both the phase separation of epigenetically similar chromatin into compartments and the expulsion of the active chromatin toward the periphery of chromosomal territories.
source: Since interactions among B-B loci result in the greatest energetic stabilization, aggregation of these loci seems to be driving force behind both the phase separation of epigenetically similar chromatin into compartments and the expulsion of the active chromatin toward the periphery of chromosomal territories.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the model results.

claim: When the epigenetic marking patterns of a locus are rewritten from A to B, the locus moves toward the interior of the chromosome, perhaps affecting the transcriptional activity of the associated genes.
source: In other words, according to the present energy landscape model, when the epigenetic marking patterns of a locus are rewritten from A to B, the locus moves toward the interior of the chromosome, perhaps affecting the transcriptional activity of the associated genes.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the energy landscape model.

claim: The MEGABASE+MiChroM computational pipeline takes chromatin immunoprecipitation tracks as input and computationally generates an ensemble of 3D structures of individual chromosomes at a resolution of 50 kb per monomeric unit.
source: We simulate the structural ensembles of chromosomes belonging to select human cell types using a previously introduced computational pipeline referred to as MEGABASE+MiChroM (Di Pierro et al., 2017). This pipeline takes chromatin immunoprecipitation tracks as input and computationally generates an ensemble of 3D structures of individual chromosomes at a resolution of 50 kb per monomeric unit.
evidence: This describes the computational methodology.

claim: The approach can be readily applied to chromosomes belonging to any cell type given epigenetic histone modification data.
source: While this approach was initially trained and validated for chromosomes belonging to human lymphoblastoid cells (GM12878), we demonstrate that this approach can be readily applied to chromosomes belonging to any cell type given epigenetic histone modification data.
evidence: This is stated as a demonstration of the generalizability of the approach.

claim: MEGABASE was trained to quantify the correlations between chromosome structural annotations with chromatin immunoprecipitation signals.
source: Maximum Entropy Genomic Annotations from Biomarkers Associated to Structural Ensembles (MEGABASE) (Di Pierro et al., 2017) was trained to quantify the correlations between chromosome structural annotations (i.e., compartment annotations A1, A2, B1, B2, B3) with chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP-Seq) signals.
evidence: This describes the training of MEGABASE.

claim: Chromatin Immunoprecipitation (ChIP-seq) data was downloaded from ENCODE for the cell lines IMR90, HUVEC, K562, HMEC, H1-hESC, and HeLa-S3.
source: Chromatin Immunoprecipitatin (ChIP-seq) data was downloaded from ENCODE (Dunham and Kundaje, 2012) for the cell lines explored in this manuscript: IMR90, HUVEC, K562, HMEC, H1-hESC, and HeLa-S3.
evidence: This describes the data sources used.

claim: The study focused on 11 histone modification tracks: H2AFZ, H3K27ac, H3K27me3, H3K36me3, H3K4me1, H3K4me2, H3K4me3, H3k79me2, H3K9ac, H3K9me3, and H4K20me1.
source: We focused on 11 histone modification tracks: H2AFZ, H3K27ac, H3K27me3, H3K36me3, H3K4me1, H3K4me2, H3K4me3, H3k79me2, H3K9ac, H3K9me3, and H4K20me1.
evidence: This describes the specific histone modifications used as input.

claim: These 11 tracks were previously shown to contain sufficient information to predict the chromosome structural ensembles for GM12878.
source: These 11 tracks were previously shown to contain sufficient information to predict the chromosome structural ensembles for GM12878 (Di Pierro et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to previous work.

claim: The polymer model is confined in a hard wall sphere to approximately preserve the volume fraction of chromatin in the interphase of 0.1.
source: The resulting polymer model is confined in a hard wall sphere to approximately preserve the volume fraction of chromatin in the interphase of 0.1 (Rosa and Everaers, 2008).
evidence: This describes a constraint in the model.

claim: All of the simulations are performed with a chromatin volume fraction of 0.1.
source: It is important to note that the simulations are not re-trained for the different cell line predictions; rather, all of the simulations are performed with a chromatin volume fraction of 0.1 (See Materials and methods for more details).
evidence: This describes a parameter used in all simulations.
